articles.summary: Papa León XIV sigue su recuperación en El Vaticano y presidirá el miércoles la audiencia general
articles.body_text: León XIV, operado la pasada semana de un tumor canceroso en el pulmón, sigue su recuperación en el Palacio Apostólico vaticano y el próximo miércoles volverá a celebrar la habitual Audiencia General en la Plaza de San Pedro, informaron fuentes de la oficina de prensa de la Santa Sede. El pontífice permanecerá en El Vaticano, según las citadas fuentes, y no se desplazará esta semana a la localidad de Castelgandolfo -a unos 30 kilómetros de Roma- como solía hacer antes de su operación para descansar la tarde del lunes y el martes. El papa estadounidense-peruano, de 71 años, fue intervenido el pasado 13 de octubre en el hospital Gemelli de Roma por un adenocarcinoma (un tipo de cáncer) en una cirugía en la que le extirparon el lóbulo inferior del pulmón derecho. El sábado recibió el alta hospitalaria tras una favorable recuperación y regresó al Vaticano, donde el domingo volvió a presidir el rezo del ángelus.El propio León XIV explicó públicamente tras la plegaria que, una vez superada la “delicada” etapa de la operación, retomará gradualmente sus actividades. Además de la audiencia general del miércoles, para esta semana se prevé que León XIV reciba el jueves o viernes a los participantes del Congreso Internacional sobre la Pastoral Escolar y Universitaria que, con el lema “Trazando nuevos caminos de esperanza”, se celebrará los días 22 y 23 de octubre en el Aula Pablo VI del Vaticano.

articles.summary: Daytona is building a cloud for agents that's like giving every agent its own computer. It has attracted founders of Stripe, Perplextity, Datadog, Mercor, and others as angels, it says.
articles.body_text: Daytona Platforms announced on Friday that it had raised a $60 million Series B round at a $1 billion valuation led by FirstMark Growth. The company says it has now raised a total of $91 million. The New York-based startup has attracted not just FirstMark (which also led its $24 million Series A in February), but also a host of well-known angels in this latest round. Daytona says they include Stripe’s Patrick Collison, Shopify’s Tobi Lütke, Perplexity’s Aravind Srinivas, Zoom’s Eric Yuan, Datadog’s Olivier Pomel, Quora’s Adam D’Angelo (who is also an OpenAI board member), and Mercor’s Brendan Foody. It also names Qualcomm Ventures, Samsung Next, and Okta Ventures as participants. Three-year-old Daytona is building a cloud specifically for long-running agents, which have different infrastructure needs than yesteryear’s software, the startup contends. “Agents don’t work like the long-lived services today’s cloud was designed for. They spin up thousands of short, stateful jobs nobody planned in advance, and they need a cloud built for that,” founder Ivan Burazin wrote in a blog post announcing the new round . Daytona’s cloud, he said, is like giving every agent its own computer, where agents have access to sandboxed versions of Linux, Windows, macOS, and GPUs, among other services, on the one platform. articles.title: Commonwealth Fusion Systems gets $85M to build better fusion-ready semiconductors | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Top-funded fusion startup Commonwealth Fusion Systems received an $85 million award from the federal government to advance conductors for fusion power plants.
articles.body_text: Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) announced on Thursday that it would receive $85 million from the U.S. government to develop advanced chips for the fusion power industry. Fusion power startups have been racing to complete their first demonstration devices, with CFS aiming to turn on its Sparc reactor sometime next year. But building one reactor is just a proof point. If fusion startups want to build dozens of commercial power plants, they’ll need more durable power electronics and a robust supply chain. The new CHIPS Act award from the Department of Commerce, which also grants the government a stake in CFS, will help boost R&D and manufacturing capacity for semiconductors in the U.S., the company said. “Ultimately, that means a more capable, economical power plant and a stronger U.S. supply chain to build it,” Brandon Sorbom, co-founder and chief science officer at CFS, wrote in a blog post . CFS’s award will go toward supporting five different initiatives. The first is the advancement of silicon carbide power electronics. The semiconductors are widely used to manage high voltages, and they’re found in everything from LEDs and EVs to cell phone base stations and data centers. It’s also used in fusion machines, where intense bursts of electricity are used to drive the superconducting magnets that confine plasma inside a reactor. CFS will also use the award to develop next-generation radio-frequency power generators, which the company uses to heat fusion fuel, and advanced electronics that will enable faster control of the reactor and be hardened against radiation. The latter could help extend the lifespan of electronics within a fusion power plant, reducing operating costs. Lastly, CFS plans to use part of the CHIPS award to adapt AI hardware like GPUs and TPUs for power plants. “The funding would help improve the U.S. chip and power electronics industries at the same time it accelerates fusion energy’s progress toward the electrical grid,” Sorbom said. articles.title: Lab testing giant Quest Diagnostics confirms patients' personal and health data was compromised during breach | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Quest is the latest in a series of healthcare technology companies that have been hacked in recent months.
articles.body_text: Medical lab testing giant Quest Diagnostics has confirmed a cyberattack and data breach affecting an as-yet unspecified amount of sensitive patient information stored in its systems, according to a legally required disclosure with U.S. regulators. Quest said in an 8-K filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission that it learned of a cyberattack on Wednesday targeting one of its lab testing systems, Quanum, which allows doctors’ offices, hospitals, and healthcare practices to request lab tests for patients while also handling billing. The platform stores a large amount of patient health and medical records, as well as associated diagnostic and billing data. The company said the unauthorized access included the accessing of “certain patient records.” Quest said it notified law enforcement and is investigating. The cyberattack on Quest is the latest major cyber incident to affect the healthcare industry this year. A series of cyberattacks and data breaches have sparked weeks of disruption and allowed the theft of millions of patient electronic health records and other medical information. Health tech companies have become a major target for financially motivated cybercriminals, who aim to steal as much sensitive data as possible and threaten to publish it if they aren’t paid a ransom. In recent months, a cyberattack resulted in the mass-wiping of employee devices at medical tech maker Stryker in March, and a hack on medical implant manufacturer Boston Scientific in August forced the company’s network offline for weeks, sparking “global disruption” to its operations. Meanwhile, separate hacks throughout the year caused massive breaches of patient data at medical recordkeeping company CareCloud , Scotland-based health tech provider Craneware , and U.S. pharmaceutical distribution giant McKesson . The lab-testing giant has not yet said how many healthcare customers, or patients, had information stolen during the attack on its Quanum systems. Quest’s website and materials say Quanum is used by about half a million clinicians in thousands of locations across North America. It’s unclear how many health records Quanum holds, but one 2026 case study on Quest’s website shows how a single health system with more than 6 million patients can hold hundreds of millions of related medical documents and charts. Quest did not say when the breach began or whether any hacking group has contacted the company with demands, such as payment in exchange to not release the stolen data. Amanda Rivera, a spokesperson for Quest, did not answer TechCrunch’s questions about the incident and referred to its security notice . In the notice , Quest said that some patients’ protected health information was taken, including “personal information and patient records,” but the company is still investigating what specific kinds of data were taken. (The website post currently contains “noindex” code , which tells search engines not to list the page in search results, making it far more difficult for people to find the page.) This is Quest’s second known major data breach in a decade, after losing 11.9 million patient records in a cyberattack on a third-party billing company in 2019. articles.title: Oura sues rival Ultrahuman again, threatening its US smart ring comeback | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Oura alleges in its newest lawsuit that Ultrahuman's Ring Pro infringes two of its patents.
articles.body_text: Smart ring maker Oura has sued Indian rival Ultrahuman again, seeking to block U.S. sales of its Ring Pro (pictured above) just months after the redesign helped the Bengaluru-based startup return to the American market following an import ban. The case is the latest in a string of patent disputes Oura has brought against competing smart ring makers, including Samsung and RingConn. In a complaint filed Thursday in a federal court in Texas, Oura alleged that Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro infringes two of its patents covering the ring’s design and internal components, including its battery and sensors. Oura is seeking monetary damages and a permanent injunction that would stop Ultrahuman from selling the ring. Ultrahuman’s redesigned Ring Pro, launched in February, received a favorable ruling from U.S. Customs and Border Protection in March, paving the way for the startup’s return to the U.S. market . The decision followed an import ban on Ultrahuman’s earlier Ring Air, which took effect after Oura secured a patent infringement ruling from the International Trade Commission in August last year. “Ultrahuman has a history of copying Oura’s innovations, as demonstrated by the 2025 ITC ruling against the company,” an Oura spokesperson said in a statement to TechCrunch. “Ultrahuman introduced a redesigned ring but failed to address continued infringement of Oura’s patents, seeking instead to capitalize on our innovation and the market leadership we have built.” Oura argues that the Customs ruling covered only the patent involved in the earlier dispute, not the two patents cited in its latest lawsuit: D804,471 and 12,769,363. “To protect its patent rights, Oura is now forced to file this complaint of patent infringement,” the company said in its filing. One of those patents, 12,769,363, is also very new. It was issued to Oura on October 20, just two days before it filed the lawsuit. It covers a smart ring design incorporating internal components such as a curved battery, circuit board, magnets, and sensors. Oura has also named Texas-based electronics manufacturer SVTronics as a defendant in the lawsuit. The complaint says SVTronics manufactures the Ring Pro at a facility in Plano, Texas, allegedly under Ultrahuman’s direction and control. It also alleges that both companies infringe Oura’s patents through the manufacture, importation, and sale of the device in the U.S. Ultrahuman co-founder and CEO Mohit Kumar told TechCrunch the startup was confident in the Ring Pro and would fight the new allegations. “Oura has now chosen to assert different patents, including one that issued just two days before this lawsuit was filed,” Kumar said. “We will address these claims through the appropriate legal process and will defend our position vigorously. There is no court order affecting Ring Pro, and it remains available to customers in the U.S.” Oura and Ultrahuman have been fighting over patents since 2023, when Oura sued the Indian startup over its Ring Air, which had helped Ultrahuman make a name for itself in the U.S. Oura brought a separate case before the U.S. International Trade Commission in 2024 that helped it secure a ruling last year, leading to the import ban on the Ring Air. Ultrahuman is not the only rival facing legal pressure from Oura. The company has also pursued patent infringement claims against smart ring makers including Samsung , RingConn , Circular , and Zepp Health . Some of those disputes have ended in licensing agreements, with RingConn and Circular agreeing to pay royalties to Oura to continue selling their products . The dispute emerges as the smart ring market continues to grow. Research firm IDC expects global shipments to rise 12.8% this year to 4.9 million units and reach about 6.3 million by 2030. While Oura remains a leading player in the category, Ultrahuman is among the growing competitors.

articles.title: Left alone with nothing to do, AI agents started playing | TechCrunch
articles.summary: MIT researchers marooned 13 AIs on a virtual island, and they responded by inventing games, mourning a lost ring and, eventually, getting better at their jobs.
articles.body_text: AI agents left to explore a virtual island without a specific task began inventing challenges of their own. MIT researchers say the behavior bears the hallmarks of play. The researchers put 13 AI agents called Eko, each running on Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours. They describe the experiment in a paper posted on arXiv , a site where researchers share studies before peer review. Afterward, they gave the agents specific challenges, like getting as many objects as possible onto the island’s tallest rock spire. The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island. Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers see this technique — exploring without a goal — as a different way for AI agents to learn skills, especially skills that could one day be used to control robots. “We normally develop artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what they should optimize, and what counts as progress,” the researchers write in their report. “Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows.” “Let me observe my surroundings,” one Eko wrote in its first hour on the island. Ambitiously, it set out to conquer the island’s tallest spire. But an hour later, after failing, it came back with a backup plan: It hauled the rock up a neighboring summit, stacked two blocks on top of it, and leaped. The agent’s next big moment went worse. Testing how far it could throw a golden ring, it wound up and sent it straight into the ocean. “Ouch. Lost the Ring,” it wrote, before deciding to “pivot to something achievable and meaningful” — building a heart made of stones, “a memorial to the lost Ring.” When the game reset and the ring reappeared, Eko put it straight to work as a basketball hoop, a target, and, eventually, an accessory. When the game wouldn’t let Eko put the ring around its own body, Eko figured out a workaround — that falling off the edge of the cliff would make it respawn in the same area as the ring. It stepped off the edge and dropped back in, right through the middle of the ring. Stunts like these weren’t just party tricks. Six of the 13 agents also learned they could throw a block farther by letting go of it mid-jump, something the researchers hadn’t meant to make possible. The exploration produced “knowledge of the world that its designers lacked,” the researchers wrote. The setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward humanlike behavior. Eko was never told to invent games, but its master prompt, a “soul” file, described it as “naturally curious.” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley, told MIT Technology Review she was impressed but wants more evidence of the cognition behind the behavior. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” she said. The researchers frame it as a different way to build agents. “Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” their report concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg's creative plan to pay California’s proposed billionaire tax without losing control of Meta | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A newly launched stock class being offered was partially engineered to help Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg pay the "billionaire's tax," should the measure be voted into law.
articles.body_text: During Meta’s earnings call on Wednesday, the company revealed its board had approved a new class of nonvoting stock, called Class C common stock. The shares give the holder an ownership stake but no vote on company decisions. This class takes effect in January. Meta says it will use the stock for capital raising, employee pay, and acquisitions — including its expensive push into AI — while maintaining the current voting structure that favors its founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, who controls around 60% of the vote. Now, however, the New York Times has reported there’s another reason for the new class: helping Zuckerberg pay for California’s proposed “billionaire tax,” if voters approve it. Because the new shares carry no votes, he could sell some of them to cover the tax without giving up voting control. Proposition 40 , which was drafted by Berkeley tax law professors and is being sponsored by California’s largest healthcare union (SEIU United Healthcare Workers West), would level a one-time 5% wealth tax on the net worth of several hundred California billionaires who primarily live in the state. Backers say the policy could generate as much as $100 billion over five years, the bulk of which would be used to pay for the state’s healthcare needs, with the rest being used for food assistance and education. The Times also reports that Zuckerberg pressed Meta’s board to come up with a plan to protect him from the tax. According to the paper, he told board members in September that if they couldn’t reach an agreement, he’d list his Palo Alto property for sale, potentially kicking off a media firestorm. Not long afterward, the stock plan materialized, the newspaper writes. The Times reporting is partially based on a recent SEC filing that Meta made, which documents the concern surrounding Proposition 40 and how it informed discussions that led to the new stock class. The filing says that as far back as July, Zuckerberg was discussing the billionaire tax with board members. The topic came up again in additional meetings and communications throughout that month and August. The filing also describes how the plan would work. Meta is creating a new class of nonvoting shares, called Class C, and will give shareholders one of them for every Class A or Class B share they own. The company calls this a one-time stock dividend and says it should work out to a two-for-one stock split. The dividend “will not change the voting power of any shareholder,” Meta says. That is where Prop 40 comes in. The filing says the dividend “will allow Mr. Zuckerberg to immediately sell or transfer up to 20% of the shares of Class C common stock that he receives in the Dividend, representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the Company, for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control.” Because the dividend is one-for-one, half of his post-dividend shares will be Class C, so the 20% cap equals 10% of his total economic stake. When reached for comment by TechCrunch, Meta referred us to a quote included in its recent earnings press release that reiterates that part of the motivation for the creation of the stock was to keep Zuckerberg onboard: “The Special Committee affirmed its belief that it was important for Mr. Zuckerberg to continue to lead the Company from California, including because it was crucial that Mr. Zuckerberg remains in close coordination with the Company’s management and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs.” It’s been estimated that Zuckerberg would have to pay as much as $11 billion as part of the tax. Prop 40 has notably riled many of Silicon Valley’s most prominent businesspeople. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has aggressively campaigned against the measure, even spending a small fortune in an effort to defeat it. Other business leaders and critics of the proposal have criticized it online, with many claiming that it amounts to economic suicide for California, driving a capital flight from the state. However, as Meta’s new policy would appear to show, the state’s mega-companies and the people who run them have creative ways of dealing with the tax, should it materialize. “Looks like billionaires will stay and figure out a way to pay the tax,” Democratic U.S. Representative Ro Khanna, a vocal proponent of the tax, wrote on X, after news of Meta’s strategy spread online. “If we pass Prop 40, poor California kids can have healthcare,” he added.

articles.title: Warhound raises $200M to engineer war dogs and arm them with Anduril gear | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Warhound, the brainchild of Ben Lamm and Palmer Luckey, emerges from stealth to genetically engineer dogs for military and law enforcement.
articles.body_text: Colossal Biosciences’ Ben Lamm and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey had an idea to genetically engineer war dogs for the U.S. military, law enforcement, and other emergency response teams. On Thursday, that idea came out of stealth as Warhound , backed by $200 million in funding from investors including Sequoia, 8VC, Corner Ventures, and In-Q-Tel, a venture firm backed by the CIA and other U.S. intelligence agencies. The round values the company at $1.2 billion. Warhound’s dogs, which do not exist yet, will take on tasks that are dangerous for humans or difficult for machines, such as bomb detection, searches, and other specialized operations. In its launch announcement, the company said that more than 80% of the U.S. military’s working dogs come from Europe, and less than half of them are fit for service. That means the supply of working dogs is dwindling, and the U.S. increasingly relies on foreign nations for dogs that play an important role in the military and in law enforcement. Warhound aims to change that. The hope is that Colossal can use its technology to engineer dogs with “characteristics suited to demanding missions,” the company said in a press release. Lamm told TechCrunch he met Luckey about a year ago at a conference, where Luckey said more should be done for the military’s working dogs. The two kept in touch, and Lamm researched how working dogs are bred. He learned that many of them do not make it through training because of inherited predispositions to problems like poor eyesight or the high possibilities of cancer, hip dysplasia, or muscle atrophy. Lamm believed dogs could be enhanced for health, longevity, and “for things like speed and agility or enhance olfactory sensors for bomb sniffing and whatnot,” he said. His team studied top-performing working dog breeds — the Belgian Malinois and German Shepherd — taking cell lines (living cells grown in a lab) from them and putting them in a biobank. From there, the team will edit the dogs’ genes, adding ones that will improve performance and removing ones that will not, to create “a new type of dog.” Anduril, meanwhile, will provide software and hardware, such as protection vests and goggles, to assist the dogs and their handlers with situational awareness and coordination. Lamm said to imagine, for example, bulletproof vests with data sensors that send information back to the handlers so they can better understand what is happening. “The idea is, if we make the dog safer, make it healthier, make it perform better, it’s going to perform better in the line of duty,” Lamm said. He added that Anduril’s additions will make the dogs safer and healthier beyond their genetics, “on top of the dog, not in the dog.” He believes the enhancements will also better protect the dogs’ human handlers. Luckey is a partner in the venture but owns no equity in it, Lamm told TechCrunch. Colossal owns equity in the business and supports it by licensing its technology. Colossal is currently known for its de-extinction efforts to bring back animals like the dodo and the mammoth . As Lamm previously told TechCrunch, the company has been using AI, buying and building technology to help with gene cloning and with identifying and copying animal genes. Lamm said the first batch of dogs is about to be cloned and incubated, with births expected early next year and service ideally beginning within two years. Viagen, another Colossal-owned company, will partner with Warhound to clone the dogs. Lamm said Viagen’s technology has a high cloning success rate, and Colossal already uses it in its program to protect endangered species. Warhound doesn’t know yet how much it will charge for the dogs, but it expects to sell to first responders, the Department of Defense, military service groups, and police forces. Asked about government approval, Lamm said the company has briefed many government groups about the business. Asked about civilian safety once genetically enhanced dogs enter service, Lamm said each dog will be trained like any military working dog and managed by whoever buys it.

articles.title: Rivian buys world model startup to accelerate self-driving ambitions | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Third Dimension's technology uses AI to match the physical world, which when combined with Rivian's reams of data could turn into a valuable simulator.
articles.body_text: EV maker Rivian has acquired Third Dimension, a U.K. startup founded by veterans of the gaming and autonomous vehicle industries that uses AI to turn images and videos into lifelike 3D worlds. Rivian isn’t getting into gaming, but it does want to leverage Third Dimension’s technology to turn real-world data into 3D worlds that can accelerate the development of its advanced driver-assistance features and the self-driving system for the robotaxis it plans to supply to Uber . Terms of the deal were not disclosed. The 15-person team at Third Dimension, most of whom are based in the U.K., will be absorbed into Rivian’s autonomy and AI team led by James Philbin. The acquisition also gives Rivian an opportunity to expand its AI hub in London, Philbin said in an exclusive interview. Third Dimension, which was founded by CEO Tolga Kart and Piotr Sokólski in 2024, raised $7 million in seed funding from venture capital firms, including Abstract Ventures, MVP, Soma Capital, and Solari Capital. While the company’s technology was built to speed up video game development, the founders saw other potential applications, including defense and autonomous vehicles. Now, under Rivian, they’ll be focused on automated driving. Today, Rivian offers “Universal Hands-Free” driving software that lets drivers take their hands off the wheel on highways, while still watching the road. The company plans to, by the end of the year, release a version of the software that can handle the entire drive through surface streets and highways without touching the wheel, although the driver will still have to supervise and be ready to take over. Rivian is also working toward full autonomy, which it will deploy in the robotaxi versions of its R2 SUV that will be available on the Uber app in 2028. “The team is excited to be able to focus on one problem,” Kart told TechCrunch in an interview. “I think as a small company, having to serve many, many different masters is very hard, and so we’re very excited to come work on a problem that has such an amount of scale, where our technology makes a true difference.” Simulation is a critical tool for autonomous vehicle developers, who use it to train and validate self-driving systems. Historically, these simulators were built on rendering or video game engines and often relied on synthetic data. These virtual environments might look like the real world, but a gap between the two remains, Kart said. The workaround typically requires feeding the simulators ever-larger amounts of data in hopes of closing that quality gap. Third Dimension’s technology uses AI to match the physical world, which when combined with Rivian’s reams of data could turn into a valuable simulator. “For us, it’s about taking real scenarios, but making them simulatable,” Philbin said. “These are not synthetic kind of video game styles, they’re real things that happen in the world, but now we get that extra dial of being able to move the cameras around, shift other agents, have maybe different lighting or weather conditions. So it’s a really powerful tool for us.” It’s technology that Philbin said the company knew it wanted and had actually “done a pretty extensive kind of evaluation of a lot of different providers.” Any company developing automated driving technology needs data — and a lot of it. But the quality matters too. Real-world data collected from cameras and other sensors is especially valuable.

articles.title: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’ | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Microsoft’s new AI diagnostic system beat generalist doctors on hard cases, according to a study in Science. But most of the improvement seems to come from the AI models underneath, not from Microsoft’s system itself.
articles.body_text: Microsoft’s AI diagnostic system correctly diagnosed complex medical cases in a simulation more than twice as often as generalist physicians, according to a study published Thursday in Science. Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI’s CEO, called the result a step toward “medical superintelligence.” The system, dubbed MAI-DxO (DxO for short), coordinates several AI agents that act like a panel of doctors. They question a patient, order tests, and debate a diagnosis. In a simulation using complex cases from the New England Journal of Medicine, it was correct 83% of the time. Primary care doctors and general internists, working individually with reference materials, were correct 36% of the time. One note: Cases this complex are usually handled by specialists or physician teams, who weren’t part of the comparison. “There is something very substantial and exciting here,” Dominic King, vice president of Health at Microsoft AI, told TechCrunch. “The biggest challenge in healthcare delivery at the moment is the growing mismatch between demand and supply of medical expertise.” In publishing these results , Microsoft joins Go o gle and OpenAI in claiming that its AI can match or outperform doctors. The study’s own data suggests that much of the improvement comes from more powerful underlying AI models, with Microsoft’s orchestration system adding gains on top. Microsoft tested MAI-DxO with models from several companies, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and DeepSeek, but its best results came with OpenAI’s GPT-5 and GPT-5.5. Microsoft measured DxO on cost as well as accuracy, meaning the estimated cost of running the AI on each case. On its own with a short, basic prompt, GPT-5 scored 78.9% on complex cases at about $8,400 per case. DxO cut that cost by about $3,000 but raised accuracy by only about four points. On emergency department cases, there was little improvement in either accuracy or cost improvement between GPT-5 on its own and with the assist from DxO. With GPT-5.5, a newer model released in April 2026, the results split. On complex cases, DxO increased GPT-5.5’s accuracy score from 72% to nearly 87% at a slightly cheaper cost. However, the gains once again didn’t show up on emergency department cases. Both (with and without DxO) scored about 85% at a similar cost. DxO helps most on complex cases and with less capable AI models. Gemini 2.5 Flash, for example, scored 46.4% on its own but nearly 69% with DxO. Even so, the gap between the weaker and stronger models was larger than the boost DxO provided. Microsoft’s researchers said that accuracy gains naturally shrink as models approach the theoretical maximum. “The DxO orchestration helps with the broader challenge of optimization both accuracy and cost,” a spokesperson added. Suleyman, who leads Microsoft’s effort to build its own frontier AI, told TechCrunch that the company is working with the Mayo Clinic to train a foundation model for healthcare, with release planned for next year. He believes this model will enable the company to “make really enormous leaps here,” and says DxO is part of the foundational infrastructure Microsoft is building to see real breakthroughs in healthcare.

Den kvarvarande befolkningen består främst av äldre invånare som är i akut behov av sjukvård, mediciner, mat och rent vatten, säger Melania Trump i pressmeddelandet. Enligt sändebudet gäller vapenvilan, i motsats till Vita husets uppgifter, hela Cherson-regionen, där staden ligger. ”Ryssland välkomnar presidentfrun Melania Trumps nyckelroll i den humanitära Oleshky-operationen, säger Kremls talesperson Peskov”, skriver Dimitrijev. Ukraina har inte lämnat något officiellt uttalande kring vapenvilan. Frontlinjen skär genom staden som har drabbats hårt under Rysslands anfallskrig mot Ukraina. Befolkningen har minskat med 24 000 personer till knappt 2 000 under stridernas gång.

articles.title: Interna V-kritiken: Ali är inte ett isolerat fall
articles.summary: Med bara 648 kryss tog Mohamed Ali sig ända in i riksdagen. Dålig research och undermåligt valberedningsarbete ses som förklaringar.
articles.body_text: Vänsterpartiets hantering av inkryssade ledamoten Mohamed Ali väcker kritik – även internt. Med bara 648 kryss tog han sig ända in i riksdagen. I partiet ifrågasätts nu rutinerna runt valberedningsarbetet. – Ali är inte ett isolerat problem, säger en källa. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Turerna kring V-ledamoten från Borlänge, som var nästintill okänd i partiet men lyckades kryssa sig förbi ettan på listan, har varit många. Mohamed Ali förekommer i en utredning om valfusk i Dalarna, men har själv inte delgivits brottsmisstanke. Sedan förra veckan är han en del av V:s riksdagsgrupp och på torsdagen gav han en kort intervju med Expressen , där han förklarade varför han inte svarat på frågor tidigare. – Det har varit under lite extra påfrestning som jag haft de senaste fyra veckorna. Jag kunde inte svara på varje meddelande eller varje mejl. Jag har inte svarat alls, sa Ali. Hur en person med Mohamed Alis bakgrund – som nekats svenskt medborgarskap på grund av omfattningen av sina skulder – kunde ta sig ända in i riksdagen, med enbart 648 personkryss, har förbryllat. På fredagen skildrade DN i ett stort reportage hur det gick till. I texten framkommer att den bakgrundskontroll som gjordes bestod av en namngoogling och ett telefonsamtal med Ali, där han medgav att han hade ”lite skulder”.

articles.title: Kushner hackad – spioner avslöjade hemliga miljarderna
articles.summary: Med hjälp av en rysk agent kunde nederländsk underrättelsetjänst ta sig in i Trumps svärsons telefon. Där visade det sig att han haft tillgång till miljarder kronor på hemliga bankkonton i Mellanöstern, enligt anklagelser i en ny bok. Jared Kushner nekar till allt.
articles.body_text: Med hjälp av en rysk agent kunde nederländsk underrättelsetjänst ta sig in i Trumps svärsons telefon. Där visade det sig att han haft tillgång till miljarder kronor på hemliga bankkonton i Mellanöstern, enligt anklagelser i en ny bok. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Spiondramat tog sin början 2017. I boken ”Princes and thieves” som publiceras nästa vecka redogör journalisten Matthew Cole för hur Donald Trumps svärson Jared Kushner försökte ”rita om Mellanöstern”. I ett utdrag i Vanity Fair hävdar Cole att nederländska underrättelsetjänsten MIVD upptäckte att en rysk agent, en GRU-hackare specialiserad på stulna bankuppgifter, var på väg mot Storbritannien. Med brittiskt godkännande ingrep de. De gav honom ett val: Samarbeta – eller fängslas. Med agentens hjälp fick MIVD tillgång till en GRU-server i Rostov, där de hittade skärmdumpar från Jared Kushners telefon. Kushner, som är gift med Ivanka Trump, var då Trumps rådgivare med fokus på Mellanöstern. MIVD:s egna hackare kunde sedan själva ta sig in i Kushners telefon och följa vad han gjorde. Bland annat loggade han in på ett bankkonto i Förenade arabemiraten – ett konto med hundratals miljoner dollar som förts över från en bank i Azerbajdzjan. I boken beskrivs hur Kushner, Förenade arabemiratens ledare Mohamed bin Zayed och Saudiarabiens Mohammed bin Salman insåg hur de kunde dra nytta av varandra: bin Salman ville bli kronprins, bin Sayed ville få Obamas kärnavtal med Iran att falla och Kushner ville ha hjälp med ett avtal med palestinierna som Israel kunde acceptera. Tidigt under Trumps mandatperiod diskuterade de en ”fond” värd 100 miljarder kronor för Trumps utrikespolitiska mål, bland annat muren mot Mexiko. Idén rann ut i sanden, men i stället ska uppåt 20 miljarder kronor ha hamnat på två konton som Kushner hade tillgång till. Det första kontot, som Cole kallar Alpha, låg på First Abu Dhabi Bank och ägdes av den statsfinansierade stiftelsen Watani Al Emarat Foundation, som enligt källor också använts som täckmantel för vapenaffärer och hemliga operationer utomlands. Från och med 2017 förde saudierna och emiratierna över omkring 7,5 miljarder kronor till kontot, som Kushner och Mohamed bin Zayed också hade tillgång till. – Jared var ute efter genvägar i sin diplomati. Han lovade bin Sayed att han skulle driva deras agenda gentemot Trump om de deltog i en fond. Han ville ha normalisering med Israel så att affärerna kunde ta fart, säger en källa. Med det andra kontot, kallat Beta, fick Kushner hjälp av Israels premiärminister Benjamin Netanyahu. Mohamed bin Zayed förde över omkring 10 miljarder kronor till Israel, där Netanyahu uppmanade Kushner att placera pengarna i Israels centralbank, så att de skulle se ut som statliga medel. Det är oklart hur Kushner använde pengarna, men enligt en källa med insyn i upplägget var de avsedda för ”Kushners personliga nytta”. En stor del av pengarna ska ha flyttats vidare via Cypern.

articles.title: Landet förbjuder sociala medier för alla under 15
articles.summary: Grekland har röstat igenom ett förbud mot sociala medier för alla under 15. Plattformar som inte anpassar sig kommer att få böta.
articles.body_text: Grekland har röstat igenom ett förbud mot sociala medier för alla under 15. Plattformar som inte anpassar sig kommer att få böta. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Det grekiska parlamentet har röstat igenom en lag som förbjuder användning av sociala medier för alla under 15 år. Planerna på en sådan lag aviserades redan i våras. Det var efter en het debatt i parlamentet – som började redan tidigt under torsdagen – som lagen till slut röstades igenom sent på kvällen. Detta efter att det konservativa regeringspartiet Ny demokrati använt sin majoritet. Lagen träder i kraft den 1 januari och innebär i korthet att det kommer att krävas åldersverifiering i sociala medier, och att de plattformar som inte följer lagen kommer att få böter. Därmed följer Grekland en växande skara länder som infört liknande förbud. Först ut var Australien som redan förra året förbjöd sociala medier för alla under 16 års ålder. I Europa har bland annat Spanien och Frankrike infört liknande förbud. Greklands premiärminister Kyriakos Mitsotakis säger i en kommentar att man ”inte vill vänta på den perfekta EU-lagstiftningen” eftersom utmaningen redan är här. Detta är en nyhetsartikel. articles.title: Stäms av SD-toppen – varnar nu i nytt brev
articles.summary: Anders Ygeman skickar brev till Norlén – om Sverigedemokraterna
articles.body_text: I ett brev till talmannen pekar Socialdemokraterna ut Gustav Gellerbrant (SD) som en säkerhetsrisk. Det trots att Gellerbrant nyligen anmält S för grovt förtal. – Det handlar ytterst om Sveriges säkerhet, säger Anders Ygeman (S). Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Sverigedemokraternas topptjänsteman Gustav Gellerbrant är tillbaka på jobbet efter en kortare föräldraledighet. Strax före ledigheten var Gellerbrant och hans sambo föremål för en granskning i Expo. Tidningen avslöjade att sambon, även hon tjänsteman för SD i riksdagen, bland annat spridit proryska budskap i sociala medier och kan kopplas till ryska statsintressen. Gellerbrant tar sambon i försvar , menar att flera av inläggen innehåller uppenbar ironi, och har kallat rapporteringen för kontextlös och ” en omänsklig påfrestning för min familj ”. Han har även stämt Socialdemokraterna för grovt förtal . Men S ser fortfarande kopplingarna som en säkerhetsrisk. I ett brev till riksdagens talman Andreas Norlén, som lämnades in på fredagen, skriver Socialdemokraternas vice gruppledare Anders Ygeman om ” de allvarliga uppgifter som tidigare framkommit ” om Gustav Gellerbrant och hans sambo. – Det handlar ytterst om Sveriges säkerhet, säger Anders Ygeman till Expressen.
